title: Two- and three-state two-color Turing machines give only repetition or nesting

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Two- and three-state two-color Turing machines give only repetition or nesting

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: All 4096 two-state, two-color Turing machines, and all of the roughly three million three-state, two-color Turing machines started on a blank tape, ultimately produce only repetitive or nested patterns.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: all ultimately turn out to yield just repetitive or nested patterns—at least if they are started with all cells white.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 3, “The World of Simple Programs”; section “Turing Machines” (from p. 78), p. 79. Scope: two-color Turing machines with two or three head states, blank initial tape

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch03-08: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.90

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Roughly three million machines are tractable with current computation and public definitions. Certification of every ultimate trajectory may require specialized proofs, but the bounded low-state space makes the reported exhaustive result checkable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate all two- and three-state two-color machines under the stated convention from blank tape, detect halting, periodic, and nested output, and use proofs or accelerated analysis for nonhalting outliers. A single machine with a non-nested, nonrepetitive ultimate pattern refutes the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Machine-count conventions and symmetry reductions must match the claim.

Ultimate behavior cannot always be certified by finite simulation alone.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.9
operationalizability: 0.85
analysis feasibility: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.95
data existence: 1.0

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Both populations are finite and completely specified: 4,096 machines are trivial, and about three million three-state machines are a modest modern enumeration. A non-nested, non-periodic survivor would refute the universal claim. The remaining care is the word 'ultimately,' which requires a long cutoff and inspection of holdouts rather than a new kind of data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate all 4,096 two-state two-color Turing machines and all 2,985,984 three-state two-color machines on a blank tape, and test whether each space-time pattern becomes periodic or nested. One machine that remains incompressible past a justified bound refutes the claim; universal regularization confirms it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
There is no single public table of all three million classifications; the check is a recomputation.

Ultimately periodic or nested can fail to show up inside a short cutoff, so long-running survivors need a separate argument.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.8
operationalizability: 0.8
data existence: 0.75
analysis feasibility: 0.72

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If the claim holds, none of the 4096 two-state and none of the 2,985,984 three-state two-colour Turing machines (NKS conventions: no halt state, head starts in state 1 on an all-white tape) produces a step sequence whose subword complexity stays high after a long transient; every machine's sequence of (head state, colour read) letters becomes eventually periodic (repetitive) or stays of low, nested-type complexity.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py evolves every two-state (4096) and three-state (2,985,984) two-colour Turing machine under the NKS numbering (p. 888) from a blank tape with the head in state 1, vectorised over chunks of 100000 machines, and records the letter sequence (state, colour read). Stage 1 computes the number p(12) of distinct length-12 factors of the letters of steps 201-1000 and flags machines with p(12) > 200 for Stage 2 (20000 steps, p(64) over steps 10001-20000; complex if p(64) >= 2500, low if <= 1280) and Stage 3 (200000 steps, p(64) over the last 100000 letters, complex if >= 25000). Periodic, Thue-Morse and uniformly random control sequences pass through the same statistics. As a supplementary (non-criterion) check the 200 highest-p(12) machines of each family are run through Stage 2 anyway, and the single highest-p(64) machine of each family is profiled at Stage-3 scale (p(n) for n = 8..512, lzma ratio, head extent and sweep lengths). Runtime about 4 minutes.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Stage 1: run every machine for 1000 steps and record the letters (state, colour read) for steps 201..1000 (alphabet 6 for s = 3, 4 for s = 2); compute the number p(12) of distinct length-12 factors of this 800-letter window; machines with p(12) <= 200 are classed low-complexity (repetitive or nested), the rest are flagged. Stage 2: run flagged machines for 20000 steps and compute p(64) over the letters of steps 10001..20000 (window of 10000; maximum possible 9937): p(64) >= 2500 is 'complex', p(64) <= 1280 (= 20 x 64, a generous linear bound for nested sequences) is low-complexity, otherwise 'unclear'. Stage 3: 'unclear' machines run for 200000 steps with the window of the last 100000 letters: p(64) >= 25000 complex, <= 1280 low-complexity, otherwise unclear. Controls run through the same statistics: a periodic letter sequence, a Thue-Morse (nested) letter sequence, and uniformly random letters, which must be classed low, low and complex respectively. PASS (supports) if no two- or three-state machine is classed complex and no machine remains unclear after Stage 3.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if at least one two- or three-state two-colour machine is classed complex at Stage 2 or Stage 3 (it is reported with its NKS number and complexity profile). MIXED if no machine is complex but some remain unclear after Stage 3, or if the controls are misclassified (criterion not discriminating).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: two- or three-state two-colour machines classed complex (or left unclear) under the pre-registered three-stage factor-complexity screen

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: exact enumeration; non-detection bounded by the 1000-step Stage-1 window

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Repetitive or nested' is operationalised through the subword complexity of the machine's step-letter sequence, which determines the whole space-time diagram given the rule: eventually periodic diagrams give bounded complexity and nested (self-similar) diagrams give complexity growing at most linearly in the factor length, whereas random-looking diagrams of the kind the book shows for four-state machines (p. 80-81) give complexity close to the window size. 'Ultimately' is bounded by the run lengths (1000, 20000, 200000 steps) with transients discarded; a machine with a transient longer than 100000 steps would be misclassed, and that limit is stated. The enumeration uses the book's numbering scheme (NKS p. 888) and its conventions (p. 78): s states, 2 colours, rule entries (new state, new colour, move +-1), blank tape, head in state 1.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: All 4096 two-state and 2,985,984 three-state two-colour Turing machines (NKS numbering) run from a blank tape, generated by analysis.py

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
No machine was flagged at Stage 1: the largest p(12) over an 800-letter window is 82 for two states and 123 for three states against a threshold of 200 (the random control gives 789 and saturates p(64) at 9937), so Stages 2 and 3 were never triggered by the pre-registered rule and the verdict follows from Stage 1 plus the controls.

Supplementary check outside the criteria: the 200 highest-p(12) three-state machines run to 20000 steps reach at most p(64) = 2021, and 72 of them fall in the pre-registered 'unclear' band 1280 < p(64) < 2500 (none is 'complex'). The top machine (number 964419) at 200000 steps has p(64) = 2243, p(512) = 15319 out of about 99500 positions, lzma ratio 0.005 (random letters: 0.39), and its head performs sweeps of lengths 3,2,2,1,1, 4,5,4,4,3,3,2,2,1,1, 6,7,6,6,5,5,..., extending the visited region by one cell per round and reaching only cells -25..24 in 20000 steps: a regular nested growth with polynomially growing factor complexity, not the saturating complexity of a random-like sequence. The two-state top machine is the binary counter 1953 (p(64) = 786, lzma 0.0025).

'Complex behaviour' is operationalised as high factor complexity of the (state, colour read) sequence; a machine whose complexity appears only after more than 1000 steps, or only in tape patterns rather than in the head's letter sequence, would be missed. The book's statement is specifically about these two families being free of class-3/4 behaviour from a blank tape, which is what is tested; the four-state machines the book exhibits as the first complex ones were not run.

Numbering follows NKS p. 888; the test does not depend on the numbering except for reporting machine numbers.
